meta.blurb: Out of breath on the stairs at forty-four, Kofi walks into a gym for the first time. His coach Ana teaches him a few basic movements, from the squat to the carry, and shows him how to add weight slowly and safely.
meta.bible: Kofi: a forty-four-year-old office worker who has never lifted weights and starts at a gym, the main character. Ana: his coach at the Riverside community gym, calm, funny and practical. Setting: Riverside Gym, a friendly gym with free weights, a few machines and a quiet corner for beginners. Key terms: Squat, Hinge, Deadlift, Press, Row, Carry, Barbell, Dumbbell, Kettlebell, Bands, Repetition, Reps, Sets, Warm-up, Soreness, Overload, Plateau, Deload, Protein, Posture, Grip, Spotter, Machines, Technique. Voice: warm, clear and encouraging, with one simple idea in each beat. The advice is general and hedged: no single programme is the best, people differ, and nothing here is a diagnosis or a personal plan. This book is general information and is not medical advice.

B1B2: Kofi is forty-four, and he sits at a desk all day. When the stairs at work leave him out of breath, he finally decides to try lifting weights.
Ana, a coach at the gym, shakes his hand and tells him that anyone can start. She explains that heavy does not mean heavy for everybody, only heavy for you today.
Strength training means making your muscles work against some kind of resistance. That can be a barbell, a pair of dumbbells, a rubber band or even your own body weight.
Strong muscles make everyday life much easier for almost everyone. They help you to carry shopping, climb stairs, stand up from a chair and play with children without feeling tired.
Muscles are not the only part of the body that benefits. Bones respond to the stress of lifting by becoming stronger, and research supports resistance exercise for keeping bones healthy.
From middle age, people slowly lose muscle if they do not use it. Strength training can slow this loss, and it is never too late to begin.
Health organisations advise adults to do muscle-strengthening activities on at least two days each week. This is in addition to walking or other exercise that raises the heart rate.
Many people worry that lifting will make them look huge, but large muscles take years of hard training and careful eating. For most beginners, the change is slow and gentle.
Before beginning, Ana gives Kofi a short form about his health. People with heart problems, chest pain, dizziness or other conditions should check with a doctor before they start lifting.
Ana says that a beginner does not need a hundred exercises. A few big movements that use many muscles at once will give him almost everything he needs.
She writes five words on the board: squat, hinge, push, pull and carry. Almost every movement we do in daily life is a version of one of these.
Ana tells him to learn the movement before adding weight. At first he will use an empty bar or a very light dumbbell, and good technique will matter more than the load.
To squat, Kofi stands with his feet about shoulder width apart and sits back and down, as if onto a chair. Then he pushes through his feet to stand up again.
Ana gives him a few simple tips for the squat, and he listens carefully. He keeps his whole foot on the floor, lets his knees follow the direction of his toes and keeps his chest lifted.
The hinge is a different movement, because the bend happens at the hips and not at the waist. Kofi pushes his hips back, keeps his back straight and feels his legs working behind him.
A deadlift is a hinge with a weight in your hands. Kofi keeps the bar close to his legs and stands up by straightening his hips and knees.
Pushing movements work the chest, the shoulders and the backs of the arms. Kofi begins with press-ups against a bench, and later he tries a light overhead press with dumbbells.
The pull is the partner of the push, and it works the muscles of the upper back. Rows help to balance the pushing movements and are good for posture.
The carry is the simplest movement of all: pick up something heavy and walk. It builds strong hands, a firm stomach and good posture, and it feels just like carrying shopping.
Before lifting, Kofi spends about five to ten minutes moving gently, on a bike or with light squats. This warms his body and helps him to feel ready for the heavier work.
Ana tells him not to hold his breath for long during a lift. A common habit is to breathe in before the effort and to breathe out as he pushes or stands.
One lift is called a repetition, or rep, and a group of reps is called a set. Many beginners start with two or three sets of about five to ten reps.
Between sets, Kofi rests for one to three minutes, and he drinks some water. Rest is not wasted time, because it lets his muscles recover enough to lift well again.
A good weight feels hard by the last few reps, but Kofi's form should still stay good. Ana likes him to finish a set feeling that he could have done one or two more.
Two or three sessions a week are plenty for a beginner, with a day of rest in between. Muscles need time between workouts to recover and to become stronger.
At his first session, Kofi's arms shake a little and the light weights feel surprisingly hard. When he finishes, however, he feels proud, because he has done what he feared.
Two days later, Kofi's legs are sore and the stairs feel difficult. This kind of soreness is common after new exercise, and it usually fades within a few days.
Soreness in the muscles is normal, but sharp pain or pain in a joint is different. If it does not go away, Kofi should stop and ask a doctor or physiotherapist.
To keep getting stronger, Kofi must ask his body to do a little more over time. This idea is called progressive overload, and it means adding weight or repetitions gradually.
Ana tells him to increase the weight in small steps. A small jump, such as a light extra plate, is much safer than a big one and is easier to repeat.
Kofi buys a small notebook and writes down the exercise, the weight and the number of reps each time. Looking back through the pages shows him how far he has come.
In the first weeks, Kofi gets stronger quickly, but not mainly because his muscles are bigger. His brain and nerves are learning how to use the muscles that he already has.
Visible changes in muscle usually take weeks or months of regular training, and they differ from one person to another. It is better to judge progress by strength than by the mirror.

Muscles need enough protein to recover after a workout and to grow. Many people can get enough from ordinary food, such as eggs, fish, beans, meat and milk, but a dietitian can give advice about individual needs.
Training uses energy, so eating enough food overall matters, as well as drinking water. Very strict dieting can leave a person weak and tired, and it makes training harder.
Muscles recover and adapt during rest, not during the workout itself. Kofi notices that when he sleeps well, he feels stronger in the gym the next day.
After a few months, Kofi's numbers stop rising for several weeks. This pause is called a plateau, and it happens to almost everyone sooner or later.
Ana suggests an easier week every now and then, which lifters call a deload. He uses lighter weights and does fewer sets, and then he returns to his normal routine.
Kofi worries that other people are watching him, but most people are busy with their own training. Good gym manners help everyone: wipe the bench, put the weights back and ask before you share.
Machines and free weights can both make you stronger. Machines guide the movement and can feel safer at first, while free weights also train balance and coordination.
A gym is helpful, but it is not necessary. At home, Kofi can use rubber bands, a pair of dumbbells, his own body weight or a backpack full of books.
For heavy lifts, such as a bench press, it is safer to use safety bars or a spotter. Kofi never lifts more than he can control just to impress anyone.
Strength training is useful for people of every age and gender. For older adults it can improve balance and help them to stay independent.
Lifting through a comfortable full range of movement can help to keep your joints flexible. Kofi notices that bending to tie his shoes has become easier.
After a workout, Kofi feels calm and proud of himself. Studies suggest that exercise, including lifting weights, can improve mood and confidence, although the effect differs from person to person.
The best programme is the one that you keep doing, week after week. If Kofi misses a session, he does not give up, but simply comes back at the next opportunity.
Three months later, Kofi carries two bags of shopping up the stairs in one trip. He is not out of breath, and he is lifting more than he ever thought he could.
Kofi's friend asks how to begin, so Kofi shows him the basics in the park. He tells him to start light, learn the movement well and add weight little by little.
There is no single best programme, and many different methods can work well. When the basics feel solid, you can explore other ideas, perhaps with the help of a qualified coach.
Start light, learn the five basic movements and add a little weight over time. This book is general information and is not medical advice, so please ask a doctor if you have any health worries.
C1C2: Kofi had spent twenty years at a desk, and the habit had settled into his body like dust into a shelf. When a single flight of stairs left him breathless and a little embarrassed, he decided at last to try lifting weights, and he stood outside the gym door for a full five minutes. At last he found the courage to open it, and he walked in with his heart beating a little faster than usual.

Ana, the coach at Riverside Gym, greeted him with a firm handshake and a cheerful lack of surprise, since she met beginners every week. She explained that lifting heavy did not mean copying the enormous weights seen on the internet, because the right load is one that is challenging for you, today, with good form. Heavy, in her gym, was a personal word, and it meant whatever was hard for the person holding the bar.

Ana walked him around the room and named what he saw: dumbbells, a barbell, kettlebells, rubber bands and a handful of machines. All of them, she said, do the same basic job, which is to make a muscle work against resistance so that it has a reason to become stronger. Even your own body weight counts, and a press-up is a perfectly respectable form of lifting.

Strength, Ana told him, is not a vanity project but a form of independence, and most of its benefits show up far from the gym. It means carrying the shopping in one trip, climbing a hill without stopping, lifting a suitcase into the luggage rack and getting up from a low chair without a groan. These ordinary tasks, she said, are what all of the lifting is really for, long after the session is over.

Muscles are only half of the story, because bones are living tissue that responds to the loads placed upon them. Research suggests that resistance exercise, along with other weight-bearing activity, helps to maintain bone strength, which matters more and more as the years go by. A bone that is never asked to work, like an unused path, slowly becomes weaker.

Most adults lose muscle mass gradually as they age, and the loss speeds up in those who are inactive. Ana explained that strength training is one of the best ways of slowing this decline, and that research on people in their seventies and eighties has shown that they can still grow stronger. It is therefore never too early or too late to begin, and Kofi's forty-four years were no obstacle at all.

Health organisations around the world, including the World Health Organization, recommend that adults do muscle-strengthening activities on at least two days each week. This is in addition to the aerobic activity, such as brisk walking, that raises the heart rate and keeps the lungs and circulation in good shape. Two sessions a week sounded to Kofi like a plan he could actually manage.

Kofi admitted to Ana that he was a little afraid of becoming enormous, a concern that she had heard from nervous beginners of every age and size. Building very large muscles, she said, takes many years of hard, focused training and a lot of food, and the usual result for a new lifter is simply a firmer, stronger and more capable body. It is a slow business, and nobody wakes up bulky by accident, however much they might sometimes wish to.

Before the first session, Ana handed him a short form that asked about his health, his medicines and any pain that he had. Anyone with a heart condition, chest pain, dizziness, a recent injury or another serious health problem should speak to a doctor before beginning, she said, and this book can give no advice about any one person's body. Kofi had no worries of that kind, but he was glad that someone had asked.

The gym was full of equipment, but Ana said that most of it was unnecessary for a beginner, and that variety is often a distraction from the work that matters. A small number of large movements that involve many muscles at the same time, such as squatting, bending, pushing, pulling and carrying, will build strength more efficiently than a dozen small, isolated exercises. Simple, she insisted, is not the same as easy, but it is far easier to learn.

On a whiteboard, Ana wrote five words in bold capitals: squat, hinge, push, pull and carry. Almost everything the human body does, from lifting a child to closing a heavy door, is some version of one of these five patterns, she said, which is why they make such a sensible foundation. Learn them well, she added, and the rest of the gym becomes a variation on a theme.

Technique comes before weight, Ana said firmly, and a beginner who lifts too much too soon is simply practising a bad habit under pressure. For the first weeks, Kofi would use an empty bar or a very light dumbbell and concentrate on moving smoothly, slowly and correctly. The weights would still be there next month, she reminded him, and so would his knees.

The squat was the first movement, and Ana had him practise it with a wooden box behind him as a target. He stood with his feet about shoulder width apart, pushed his hips back, lowered himself slowly and then drove up through his feet until he was standing tall. It was, as she pointed out, simply what a healthy person does every time he sits down and stands up, but done deliberately and with attention.

She offered a handful of simple reminders: keep the whole foot flat on the floor, let the knees travel in the same direction as the toes, keep the chest lifted and the eyes forward, and breathe steadily throughout. None of this is a rule from heaven, she said, because bodies differ and the exact shape of a good squat varies from person to person. What matters most is that the movement feels strong and controlled, and that it does not cause any pain.

The second pattern, the hinge, felt strange to Kofi at first, because he had always bent over from the waist like most office workers. Ana showed him how to push his hips back as though closing a car door with them, keep his back long and straight, and let his upper body tip forward as a single unit. He felt the muscles along the back of his legs working hard, and he realised that he had barely used them for years.

Once he had mastered the hinge with an empty bar, Ana let Kofi try a deadlift, which is simply the movement of lifting a weight from the floor to a standing position. She told him to keep the bar close to his body, brace his stomach, keep his back flat and stand up by straightening his hips and knees together. It felt like the most natural thing in the world, which is perhaps why it is so useful, since we spend our lives picking things up.

The push, in its many forms, trains the chest, the shoulders and the backs of the arms, and the easiest way to start is with a press-up against a sturdy bench. As his strength increased, Kofi progressed to the floor and later to pressing a pair of light dumbbells above his head, always with his stomach firm and his ribs down. Each variation, Ana said, is the same basic idea at a different level of difficulty.

Ana was particularly keen on the pull, because most people spend their days hunched forward over a keyboard and so neglect the muscles of the upper back entirely. Rows, in which the weight is drawn towards the body, strengthen exactly those muscles and balance the work of the pushing movements. A body trained to push and pull in equal measure, she said, is more even and often more comfortable.

The carry was the simplest pattern of all, and Kofi was almost disappointed by how little instruction it needed: pick up two heavy weights, stand tall and walk. It trained his grip, his shoulders, his stomach and his balance in one go, and it felt remarkably like carrying shopping bags in from the car, which is exactly the point. Strength that is built in the gym, Ana said, should be strength that you can use outside it.

Before every session Ana asked Kofi to spend about five to ten minutes warming up, pedalling gently on a stationary bike, swinging his arms and practising a few light squats. A warm-up raises the body temperature, loosens the joints and, perhaps just as important, tells the mind that the real work is about to begin. Researchers are still debating how much it protects against injury, but most people find that they simply feel better afterwards.

Many beginners hold their breath while lifting without noticing, which can leave them dizzy and push up their blood pressure for a moment. Ana taught Kofi a steadier habit, which was to take a breath before the hard part of the movement and to let it out as he pressed or stood up. If he ever felt faint or unwell during a lift, she added, he should put the weight down at once.

Ana taught Kofi the language of the gym: a single lift is a repetition, or rep, and a group of repetitions performed without a pause is a set. Many beginner programmes use two or three sets of roughly five to ten repetitions for each exercise, although researchers have found that a wide range of schemes can build strength, and no single combination is the correct one. What matters, she said, is that the work is hard enough and that you actually do it.

Kofi had assumed that the harder he worked, the less he ought to rest, but Ana taught him that the pauses are part of the training. Between heavier sets, most people need about one to three minutes for their muscles and breathing to recover well enough to lift with good form again. Rushing the rest, she warned, just makes the next set worse and the whole session less useful.

How heavy is heavy enough, Kofi wanted to know, and Ana gave him a rule of thumb that has served many beginners well. The last repetitions of each set should feel challenging, but his technique should remain good, and he should finish with the sense that he could have managed one or two more. Training to the point of collapse is unnecessary for a newcomer, she said, and it makes the form untidy and the risks higher.

Kofi's plan was a modest one: three sessions a week, on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, with the days in between left free for walking, stretching or doing nothing in particular. Muscles do not become stronger during the lifting itself but during the recovery that follows it, Ana explained, and a body that is never allowed to rest only becomes tired. Two sessions a week, she added, would still be a good start if three felt like too much.

His first session was humbler than he had imagined, with an empty bar, a light dumbbell and a great deal of concentration, and his arms trembled slightly by the end. Yet when he sat in the car park afterwards, he felt a quiet, unfamiliar satisfaction, the kind that comes from doing something difficult that you were afraid to start. It was only the beginning, but the beginning, he realised, was the hardest part.

On the second morning, Kofi came down the stairs like a man of ninety, gripping the rail and complaining to the empty hallway. Ana had warned him that muscle soreness, which tends to peak a day or two after unfamiliar exercise, is common and normally eases within a few days, and that gentle walking often helps. It was strangely satisfying to feel the places where the work had been done.

Ana was careful to separate two kinds of discomfort: the dull ache of tired muscles, which is a normal part of training, and sharp, sudden or lasting pain, especially in a joint, which is not. If the second kind appears, she said, the sensible response is to stop that exercise and to seek advice from a doctor or a physiotherapist, rather than to push on and hope. A body complains for a reason, and it is always wise to listen carefully before deciding to ignore it.

The central principle of all strength training, Ana told him, is progressive overload: to keep improving, the body must be asked to do slightly more than it is used to. That extra demand might take the form of a little more weight, an additional repetition or a slightly better quality of movement, and the body responds by adapting. Without this gradual increase, she said, the body has no reason to change and the progress simply stops.

Kofi was tempted to leap forward, but Ana urged him to climb the ladder one rung at a time, adding the smallest plates available when a weight felt comfortable for all of his sets. Small, regular increases are safer and easier to sustain than occasional dramatic leaps, and over many weeks they add up to something impressive. A tortoise, she observed with a smile, is a perfectly good model for a lifter.

Ana recommended that Kofi keep a simple record, noting the exercise, the weight and the number of repetitions every time he trained. Memory is unreliable and progress is often too gradual to notice from one week to the next, but a notebook shows plainly that the weight on the bar has grown. Reading back through the pages, he found, was one of the most motivating parts of the whole process.

Within a few weeks Kofi was lifting noticeably more than at the beginning, and he was puzzled, since his arms looked no different in the mirror. Ana explained that early gains come largely from the nervous system learning to recruit the muscle that already exists, so the movement becomes smoother and more efficient before much new muscle has been built. Real growth follows more slowly, and it is measured over months and years rather than over weeks.

Muscles grow more slowly than most beginners expect, and visible changes usually appear after many weeks or months of regular training and adequate food. The pace differs widely from person to person, depending on age, genes, sleep and the kind of training done, so comparing yourself with a stranger in a photograph is an unprofitable exercise. A better measure, Ana suggested, is whether the lifts on your page are slowly rising.

Muscles are built partly from protein, and a person who trains regularly needs enough of it to repair and build tissue between sessions. Most people can find what they need in ordinary food such as eggs, fish, poultry, beans, lentils, dairy products and tofu, and expensive powders are not usually necessary. Anyone with a medical condition, or with special needs, should ask a doctor or a dietitian for personal advice before changing how they eat.

Lifting is hungry work, and Ana pointed out that a body which is short of energy will find it harder to train, to recover and to build strength. Eating regular meals with enough food overall and drinking water through the day will support the work, whereas extreme dieting tends to leave a lifter weak, tired and frustrated. Strength grows best, she said, in a body that is properly fed, properly rested and properly looked after.

After a few weeks of training, Kofi noticed that his best sessions nearly always followed a good night's sleep and his worst ones a bad night. Sleep is one of the main times when the body repairs itself and consolidates what it has learned, and research links poor sleep with poorer recovery and lower energy. A training plan, he began to see, does not stop at the door of the gym.

Around the fourth month, the numbers in Kofi's notebook stopped rising, and for three weeks the same weight stared back at him from the page. Such a plateau is normal and happens to almost every lifter, Ana reassured him, and it often responds to better sleep, more food, smaller jumps in weight or simply a little more patience. It does not mean that anything has gone wrong, only that the easy gains have been used up.

Ana also suggested an occasional lighter week, which lifters call a deload, in which the weights are reduced and the sets are fewer. Many coaches believe that such a pause lets accumulated fatigue fade and helps the body to come back stronger, although there is no single schedule that suits everyone. It felt like cheating at first, but Kofi returned from his easy week fresher and, surprisingly, a little stronger.

Kofi had feared that the regulars would stare at the newcomer in the old T-shirt, but he soon found that most people were far too occupied with their own training to notice him. Ana told him that every strong person in the room had once been a beginner and that the unwritten rules were simple: wipe down the bench, return the weights to the rack and ask politely before sharing equipment. Courtesy, it turns out, is much the same in every gym and in every other place where people share space.

Kofi asked whether machines were somehow cheating, and Ana laughed and told him that both machines and free weights can build strength effectively. Machines guide the path of the movement and can feel reassuring to a beginner, whereas free weights demand more balance and coordination and are closer to what we do in daily life. A sensible programme, she said, can make good use of both, and many experienced lifters do exactly that.

When a busy week made the gym impossible, Kofi discovered that he could train just as well in his living room with the tools that he already had. A rubber band, a pair of dumbbells, his own body weight and a backpack filled with books were enough to practise every one of the five patterns, as Ana had promised. The best place to train, she liked to say, is the one where you will actually turn up.

As the weights became heavier, Ana introduced Kofi to the safety equipment that every gym provides, such as adjustable safety bars and the help of a spotter, a person who stands ready to assist if a lift fails. She also made him promise never to lift more than he could properly control simply to impress someone, since ego is the most dangerous weight in the building. A sensible lifter respects the bar and the people around it, and leaves the showing off to others.

Kofi noticed that Ana's classes held people of every age, shape and background, including a grandmother in her seventies who deadlifted with a quiet smile. Research supports strength training for women and for older adults, not least because stronger muscles can improve balance, reduce the risk of falls and help people to remain independent for longer. The idea that lifting is only for young men, Ana said, is a myth that needs retiring.

Kofi had assumed that lifting would make him stiff, so he was surprised to find that he could bend down and touch his toes more easily than a year earlier. Studies suggest that strength training, when it is done through a comfortable full range of movement, can improve flexibility about as well as stretching in some people. Strength and flexibility, it seems, are friends and not rivals, and Kofi was happy to enjoy them both.

Over the months, Kofi noticed a change that had nothing to do with muscle: he stood a little taller, worried a little less and felt more capable in everyday life. Studies suggest that regular exercise, including strength training, is associated with better mood and with lower anxiety for many people, though the size of the effect varies and exercise is not a substitute for proper care when someone is unwell. For Kofi, the weights had become a small daily proof that he could do hard things.

Ana's most repeated piece of advice was that consistency beats intensity: a modest programme that is followed for years will always outperform a heroic one that is abandoned in a month. When Kofi missed a week because of a cold and a deadline, he returned with a little guilt, and she waved it away and handed him a pair of dumbbells. Nobody who lifts for a lifetime lifts every single day, and a short break is a normal part of the story.

Three months after that nervous first morning, Kofi carried two heavy bags of shopping up the stairs to his flat in a single trip and arrived at the top without a gasp. His notebook told the same story, for the weight on the bar had risen steadily from the empty bar to an amount that would once have terrified him. The change had been gradual enough to go unnoticed day by day, but undeniable when he looked back.

When a friend at work asked how Kofi had changed so much, he found himself repeating Ana's words in a park, with a wooden box and a backpack for equipment. Start light, learn the movements, add a little at a time and keep turning up, he said, and then he watched his friend squat for the first time with the same look of concentration that he had once worn himself. It felt good to pass on something that had been given to him, and to see it passed on again.

As his confidence grew, Kofi began to read about other approaches, from machines to kettlebells to bodyweight skills, and found that each of them had enthusiastic supporters. Ana smiled at his discovery, and told him that no programme is the best for everyone, and that once the basic movements feel solid there is plenty of room to explore, ideally with the guidance of a qualified coach. The foundation is what counts, she said, and everything built on top of it is only decoration.

To begin lifting, you need only a light weight, a few basic movements, a little patience and the willingness to add a little at a time and to keep turning up. Every strong person you will ever meet began as a beginner, and Kofi's story, like yours, started with a single open door. This book is general information and is not medical advice, so please talk to a doctor or a qualified coach about your own body and your own needs.
